title: Problems that retrieval augmentation can solve

opening.headline: You will learn how to fill in the latest information and in-house knowledge that the model does not know through search, and the boundaries of problems that search cannot solve.
body: The model does not know about internal documents or recently changed procedures that it has never trained on. Still, because the model confidently answers plausible generalities, it is difficult to detect that it is wrong.

In this class, we will look at how Search Augmented Generation (RAG) solves unknown problems. We also distinguish between the impact of search quality and context length on results, and the difference between cases where the search is wrong and is wrong and cases where the search is correct but is wrong.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the problem that search augmentation solves
Distinguish between search and generation problems

screens.title: The model does not know our company knowledge
screens.lead: This is a scene where an employee asked a question to an in-house chatbot. Read the questions and answers in turn and think about what the problem is.

visual.alt: A scene where the user's question speech bubble and the model's general answer speech bubble are placed face to face.
labels: What is the return process that changed last quarter?
Returns are generally accepted within 14 days with receipt.

paragraphs: An employee asks an in-house chatbot. 'What is the return process that changed last quarter?' The model answers without hesitation. It's a nice description of the typical returns process, but it doesn't say a single line has changed in the last quarter.

The reason is that the model has never been trained on any in-house documents. OpenAI's Accuracy Optimization Guide outlines three cases where context optimization is needed: This is when the information was not in the training data, when the model's knowledge is out of date, or when private information is needed. This case applies to all three.

This problem cannot be solved by refining the directive. Because there's no way to get a model to tell you something it doesn't know. This lesson distinguishes how search augmentation solves these problems and which problems it cannot solve.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: There is no indication that the model's answer is wrong. So how can we filter out unfounded answers?

screens.outro: Let’s think about whether there is a similar situation in your work.

screens.title: Think about in-house knowledge that the model does not know
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit an answer, so think of your task first and then press it.

items.prompt: Are there any tasks that require in-house knowledge that the model does not know about?
items.answer: Representative knowledge is not disclosed to the outside world, such as customer service procedures, product specifications, and internal policies. Since this knowledge has not been learned by the model, it must be passed as input before it can be used in the answer.

items.prompt: Where does that knowledge reside: in documents, wikis, databases?
items.answer: Storage location and format are the starting point when designing search augmentations. The document must be broken into pieces and the database must be retrieved with a query. Remember, you can't retrieve knowledge you don't know where it is.

items.prompt: How often does that knowledge change?
items.answer: The more frequently the knowledge changes, the more appropriate it is to pass it as input rather than putting it into the model. This is because the input can be changed for each request, but the content learned in the model is not easily updated.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's take a step-by-step look at the flow of search augmentation.

screens.title: Flow of RAG: Find, attach, answer
screens.lead: Select a number marker to see a detailed description of that step. Please press numbers 1 to 5 in order.

visual.alt: A horizontal pipeline starting from a question, through embedding, retrieval, prompt injection, and generation, and a knowledge store underneath.

markers.label: question
markers.title: User questions come in
markers.body: The flow starts with a question from the user. Rather than going straight to the model, questions first go through a knowledge repository. RAG is a way to enrich a prompt by finding relevant content before creating it. So the name is Generation augmented with Retrieval.

markers.label: Embedding
markers.title: Transform knowledge and questions into embeddings
markers.body: In the preparation phase, the entire knowledge is divided into small pieces, or chunks, of a few hundred tokens or less. Convert each chunk into a vector containing meaning using an embedding model and save it. When a question comes in, we embed it in the same way. Comparing two vectors allows us to calculate how close their meanings are.

markers.label: search
markers.title: Find the closest piece
markers.body: Find the chunk in the vector store that is closest in meaning to the question's embedding. The results of this step are the basis on which the model will soon be seen. The OpenAI documentation explains that RAG introduces a new optimization axis called search. If this step is wrong, no matter how good the subsequent steps are, they are of no use.

markers.label: injection
markers.title: Insert the found fragment into the prompt
markers.body: Place the chunks you find into a prompt with a question. This is the moment when knowledge becomes part of the input. The model itself doesn't change, but the inputs change, so the answer changes. This is context injection.

markers.label: create
markers.title: The model looks at the evidence and answers
markers.body: The model creates an answer based on the evidence provided in the prompt. In the previous example, the changed return procedure document is input, so you can answer the actual procedure instead of the general theory. If the answer is still wrong, you need to distinguish whether the search was wrong or the model on which you received the evidence was used incorrectly.

screens.outro: Now that you understand the flow, let's see how search quality and context length affect the results.

screens.title: Search quality and context length
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the number of chunks you put in your prompt. You can see whether the more you put in, the better it gets, and where the limits are.

visual.alt: A side-by-side illustration of a list of retrieved chunks and a bar showing how much goes into the prompt.
labels: How much goes into the prompt

data.controlLabel: Number of chunks to put in the prompt

stops.body: If your entire body of knowledge is smaller than about 200,000 tokens, or about 500 pages of documentation, it's simplest to put the entire thing in the prompt without a RAG. Anthropic explains that prompt caching makes this method much faster and more economical. If your knowledge is smaller than this, consider this approach first before building your search pipeline.

If your knowledge is too large to include in its entirety, include only a few high-level chunks that are close to the question. Entering only 5 makes the input short and easy for the model to read, but if the required chunk is outside the top 5, the model will never see that information.

Increasing the number of chunks to 10 increases the likelihood that they will contain the information you need. Instead, less related pieces come in as well. The more pieces you have, the longer the input and the more the model has to look at.

In Anthropic's experiment, when 5, 10, and 20 were compared, 20 performed best. This is because adding more chunks increases the likelihood of receiving relevant information. However, results may vary for each use case, so we encourage you to experiment with the documentation as well.

More information is not always better. The Anthropic document explains that there are limitations as too much information can distract the model. The OpenAI document also states that if there is a lot of irrelevant content, real information may be buried and hallucinations may increase. How much to put in is determined by evaluation.

screens.outro: Now let's move on to an explanation of the distinction between search failures and creation failures.

screens.title: Explanation: Cases where the search is correct but incorrect, and cases where the search is incorrect and is incorrect.
screens.lead: The instructor diagnoses both cases in the same order. Select the right arrow to skip a step. Learners do not enter answers.

steps.title: Can break in two places
steps.body: The OpenAI documentation explains that RAG applications can break in two places: One is Search and the other is LLM. If the search is incorrect, the model cannot answer, and even if the search is correct, the model may use the evidence incorrectly. If you don't distinguish between the two, your prescriptions will get mixed up.

steps.title: Case A: Looking at the context that went into the model first
steps.body: The chatbot answered with the previous return procedure. Diagnosis begins with looking at the context that went into the model, not the sentences written by the model. When I opened the search results, I found that the changed procedure documents did not come in and older documents were at the top.

steps.title: Case A: The search is incorrect.
steps.body: If the wrong context is entered, the model cannot answer. The prescription is to fix the search. Tuning your search to produce the right results, tuning it to reduce noise, and enriching each result to contain more information. In this case, changing or tuning the model instructions has no effect.

steps.title: Case B: The context is correct but the answer is wrong
steps.body: In the second case, the model responded with a mix of old and new procedures, even though the changed procedure document was entered correctly. Search is successful and creation is failed. Even though the model was given the correct context, it did something wrong.

steps.title: Case B: Prescription is Improving Instructions
steps.body: The OpenAI documentation advises in this case to improve the instructions and methods used by the model. For example, it clearly states that answers should be based only on information in the documents provided, and that if there are conflicting documents, the most recent document should be followed. If the accuracy improves by showing an example, we will consider tuning.

steps.title: The first step in diagnosis
steps.body: In both cases, the answer appeared to be incorrect, but the prescriptions were different. The key to distinction is to first determine which context went into the model. If the entered context is incorrect, it is a retrieval problem, and if it is correct but the answer is wrong, it is a generation problem.

screens.outro: Finally, let's look at the signals that indicate search failure one by one.

screens.title: Read search failure signals
screens.lead: The following cards show four signs that a search has failed: When you select a card, it flips over to reveal candidate causes and ways to check. Select the right arrow to advance to the next card.

visual.alt: Card front icon with magnifying glass and document fragment.
labels: The standard answer is clearly in the document, but it doesn't appear in the top results.
Top results are filled with only similar pieces of the same topic
By itself, it is impossible to tell which company and period it belongs to.
No matter how much I increase the result, the pieces I need don't come in.

cards.front: The standard answer is clearly in the document, but it doesn't appear in the top results.
cards.back: Candidate causes are cases where the semantic search misses a result because the wording of the question and the document are different. The way to check is to directly open the top results with a few evaluation questions. For identifiers that require an exact match, lexical matching such as BM25 can complement semantic search.

cards.front: Top results are filled with only similar pieces of the same topic
cards.back: When similar pieces monopolize the top, there is less room for information from different perspectives. The method of checking is to check for duplicates in the result list. Reduce the noise in your search results and adjust them to include diverse pieces.

cards.front: By itself, it is impossible to tell which company and period it belongs to.
cards.back: This is a case where context is lost while dividing chunks. For example, the piece that says 'Sales increased by 3% compared to the previous quarter' is difficult to find and write because it is unclear which company and which quarter it is from. There is a way to add context to a fragment.

cards.front: No matter how much I increase the result, the pieces I need don't come in.
cards.back: There are limits to ways to increase the number. The more there is, the more likely the model will become distracted and hallucinate. If adjusting the number does not solve the problem, you will need to change the way the pieces are divided or searched. These signals are solved through search-side refinement and not through model tuning.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to read the signals, we'll summarize the entire lesson in the final screen.

screens.title: Context problems are solved through search
screens.lead: Structure the answer to the question asked at the beginning and how to use in-house knowledge that the model does not know in the answer.

paragraphs: The chatbot in the first scene did not know the changed return procedure. This is a problem of the context axis, and search augmentation solves this by finding relevant content and putting it in the prompt before creation. The model remains the same, but the inputs change, so the answer is different.

The effectiveness of context injection depends on two things. One is search quality. If the wrong context is entered, the model cannot answer, and if there is a lot of irrelevant information, the real information is buried. The other is context length. If the knowledge is less than about 200,000 tokens, it is simplest to insert the whole thing, and if it is larger than that, only the top pieces are selected and inserted.

Failure due to incorrect retrieval and failure due to incorrect creation have different prescriptions. If the search is incorrect, we adjust the search, and if the context is correct but the answer is incorrect, we improve the instructions. Without this distinction, time is lost trying to solve search problems with directed refinement.

To summarize, the structure of this class is as follows. First, check whether it is an unknown problem, and if it is an unknown problem, inject context through search. Even after injection, if it is incorrect, check which context was entered and determine which part of the search or creation was broken.

Another thing to remember is that RAG does not teach the model new knowledge. The model is the same, just the prompts are based on the evidence. So, if your knowledge changes, you only need to change the documents in the repository without retraining the model.

To apply the contents of this class in practice, you need to check three things. Where the necessary knowledge is located, whether it is large enough to be included in its entirety, and whether the context that went into the model can be checked when an incorrect answer is given.

callout.label: Based on one sentence
callout.text: If you don't know something, put it into context by searching, and check the context for the wrong answer first.

checks.intro: Check for yourself by recalling the context length criteria you just saw. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: The total amount of in-house knowledge is small enough to be inputted into the model at once. What's the simplest way?
options: Build a RAG pipeline that selects only the top few pieces.
Put your entire knowledge directly into the prompt
Convert knowledge into learning data and tune it
Discard all chunks and use only BM25
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. If the knowledge is small, it is simplest to put it all in without a pipeline.
checks.incorrectFeedback: That method is either more complicated or not fit for purpose. Recall how knowledge size changes choices.
checks.explain: If your knowledge is less than about 200,000 tokens, it is simplest to put it all in the prompt. When it is bigger, you need a RAG that only puts the parent fragment.

wrong.0: RAG is a method needed when knowledge is greater than the input limit.
wrong.2: Tuning is not suitable for knowledge injection and is expensive.
wrong.3: Changing search methods is not the answer to the size problem.

checks.intro: Think of the two failures you saw in the commentary and match the situation with the prescription. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match prescriptions with situations that appear in search augmentation
left: The model cannot answer because the context is incorrect.
The context is correct, but the model behaves incorrectly.
Semantic search misses items that require an exact match, such as identifiers
right: Complemented with vocabulary matching such as BM25
Search tuning, noise reduction, and information enrichment per result
Improve instructions and tune if examples are helpful.
checks.correctFeedback: The prescriptions for all three situations were appropriate.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some prescriptions were violated. Again, try to determine whether the problem is with search or creation.
checks.explain: RAG can be broken in both search and creation places, and the prescriptions are different. For items that require an exact match, lexical matching complements semantic search.

checks.intro: Remember the contents of the signal card and check the last question. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: The standard answer is clearly in the document, but no matter how much I increase the search results, the fragment does not appear at the top. What is the appropriate response?
options: Tune the model to memorize the answer
Summarize the answers and use them as learning examples.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. This is a problem of not being able to find the required piece, so it must be solved on the search side.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The response does not get to the cause. Look again at the step where the problem occurred.
checks.explain: Since this signal is a problem of not finding the piece that needs to be searched, it is solved by improving the search, not by model tuning.

wrong.0: It is not appropriate to require knowledge to be memorized in the model, and it does not reflect the latest changes.
wrong.1: If the necessary pieces are not in the input, no matter how much you refine the instructions, you cannot come up with an answer.
wrong.2: Using it as a training example does not solve the cause of search failure.

glossary.def: It stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. This method searches for related content and attaches it to the prompt before generating an answer.
Information that the model does not know is directly entered into the input. The model does not change, but the input changes and the answer changes.
These are small pieces of text that break up a document for search. It is usually divided into a few hundred tokens or less.
A vocabulary-based function that ranks based on exact word matches. It is especially effective for queries containing unique identifiers or technical terms.
This is the stage where many candidates collected through search are re-evaluated based on their relevance to the query and only the top few are selected.

misconceptions.myth: When you attach a RAG, the model learns new knowledge.
misconceptions.fact: The model is the same, just the prompts are based on the evidence. If the evidence disappears from the input, the model will not know that knowledge again.

misconceptions.myth: The more search results, the better the answer.
misconceptions.fact: An increase in irrelevant content can cause hallucinations to increase as important information gets buried. How much to put in must be determined through evaluation.

misconceptions.myth: If the answer is wrong, it's a search problem.
misconceptions.fact: Even if the search is correct, the model may use the context incorrectly. Search and creation are diagnosed separately by first checking the context entered into the model.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: If you don't know a problem, use a search to find related information and solve it by typing it into the prompt.
Search quality and context length determine the effectiveness of context injection.
Failure due to incorrect retrieval and failure due to incorrect creation have different prescriptions.
If your knowledge is small, it is simplest to include it in its entirety.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: In our work, where does the context that a model needs to know come from, how often does it change, and how should it be conveyed to the model?
